title: The Broken Heart
text:
People have long spoken of dying of a broken heart. In the 1960s, the British psychiatrist Colin Murray Parkes, who studied grief, worked with the statisticians Bernard Benjamin and R. G. Fitzgerald to test the idea with hard numbers.

They identified 4,486 widowers aged 55 and older in England and Wales whose wives had died in 1957, and followed them for nine years using official death records. They compared the men's death rates with those of married men of the same age in the general population.

The first six months after bereavement stood out. During that period, the widowers' death rate was about 40 percent higher than expected. After that, it fell back toward the normal rate for their age. The largest part of the excess came from heart disease, including coronary thrombosis and other circulatory conditions, which led the authors to title their paper "Broken Heart."

The researchers considered several explanations: that husband and wife might share an unhealthy environment, or that the stress of grief itself might strain the body. The pattern, concentrated in the early months, was more consistent with the effects of grief. Later studies in other countries found similar spikes in mortality after the death of a spouse.
lesson: The months after losing a partner are a time of real physical danger, not only sorrow. Stay close to the bereaved and watch their health.
people: Colin Murray Parkes, Bernard Benjamin, R. G. Fitzgerald
source: Parkes, C. M., Benjamin, B., and Fitzgerald, R. G. (1969). Broken heart: A statistical study of increased mortality among widowers. British Medical Journal, 1(5646), 740-743.
